meta.name: Brussels Griffon First Year Costs
meta.excerpt: Brussels Griffons are not cheap to acquire, and ongoing grooming, dental, and potential health costs add up. Here is a realistic first-year cost breakdown for this devoted little Belgian breed.
meta.meta_description: Brussels Griffon first year costs: puppy price, grooming, vet care, and ongoing annual expenses for this small Toy breed.

intro.label: Upfront Costs
intro.heading: Higher Than Average Toy Breed Acquisition Costs
intro.html:
The Brussels Griffon is a relatively rare breed and quality puppies command prices reflecting that scarcity along with the costs of health testing. Litter sizes tend to be small (1–4 puppies is common), and Cesarean sections are frequently required due to the puppy's large head relative to the dam — both of which increase breeder costs that are passed to buyers.

  • Puppy from health-tested breeder: $1,500–$3,000. Rare colors or show-quality lines may exceed this range.
  • Initial vet visit and puppy vaccines: $150–$300
  • Spay or neuter (small breed): $200–$400
  • Crate (medium or large for comfort): $50–$100
  • Small breed food and water bowls: $20–$50
  • Collar, harness, and leash: $40–$80 (a harness is recommended over collar-only for brachycephalic breeds to reduce neck and airway pressure)
  • ID tag: $10–$20
  • High-quality small-breed puppy food (first months): $60–$120
  • Puppy classes: $100–$200
  • Grooming tools or first professional groom: $50–$150

Upfront total estimate: $2,180–$4,420

care.label: First Year Recurring
care.heading: Monthly and Annual Expenses
care.html:
The Brussels Griffon is inexpensive to feed but regular grooming — especially for rough coats — and dental care create meaningful ongoing costs.

  • Food (small-breed kibble or mixed diet): $30–$60/month. Annual cost: $360–$720.
  • Professional grooming (rough coat clip every 6–8 weeks): $50–$90 per session, 6–8 sessions/year. Annual grooming cost: $300–$720. Smooth coats require much less professional grooming.
  • Routine vet visits and puppy vaccines: $250–$450 in the first year
  • Heartworm/flea/tick prevention: $80–$150/year (small breed)
  • Pet insurance: $25–$50/month for a small breed. Given the potential for eye, airway, and neurological conditions, coverage is worthwhile. Annual cost: $300–$600.
  • Dental chews and home dental care supplies: $50–$100/year
  • Toys and accessories: $80–$150/year

First-year recurring total (with insurance): $1,420–$2,890

special.label: Total & Ongoing
special.heading: Full Year One and Annual Budget
special.html:
Total first-year estimate (with insurance): $3,600–$7,310

Annual ongoing costs after year one:

  • Food: $360–$720
  • Professional grooming: $300–$720 (rough coat) or $0–$200 (smooth coat)
  • Routine vet care: $200–$400
  • Heartworm/parasite prevention: $80–$150
  • Pet insurance: $300–$720 (increases with age)
  • Dental care (professional cleanings recommended annually): $200–$500
  • Miscellaneous: $100–$200

Estimated annual ongoing total: $1,540–$3,090

Potential additional health costs:

  • BOAS surgical correction (if needed): $1,500–$4,000
  • Eye surgery or ongoing medication (dry eye, corneal issues): $300–$1,500
  • Syringomyelia treatment (if diagnosed): $500–$3,000+ depending on severity

These are not certain costs, but the Brussels Griffon's health profile makes them worth budgeting for contingently or covering with pet insurance.

faq.q: Why are Brussels Griffon puppies so expensive?
faq.a: Litter sizes are typically very small (1–4 puppies), Cesarean sections are often required due to the puppy's large head, and reputable breeders invest in health testing including MRI screening for syringomyelia. These factors combine to make puppies relatively expensive for their size.

faq.q: Is the rough coat or smooth coat Brussels Griffon more expensive to own?
faq.a: The rough coat is more expensive due to professional grooming costs (regular clipping or stripping every 6–8 weeks). The smooth coat requires little professional grooming.

faq.q: Do Brussels Griffons need dental cleanings?
faq.a: Yes. The brachycephalic jaw crowds teeth into a small space, making dental disease more likely than in longer-muzzled breeds. Most Brussels Griffons benefit from annual professional dental cleanings and daily home brushing.
